After examining how LLM agents can support ticket handling, the next question is how to measure
whether these models are actually effective in O&M scenarios. Evaluation is important because
O&M tasks require domain knowledge, accurate troubleshooting, reliable recommendations,
and consistent performance across areas such as infrastructure, databases, networks, operating
systems, and security.
Evaluating LLM capabilities for O&M
The core value of intelligent O&M lies in leveraging artificial intelligence to replace manual
decision-making, quickly provide troubleshooting suggestions, or prevent faults in advance.
Intelligent O&M revolves around big data and algorithm platforms, extracting data from various
monitoring systems, offering services to users, and incorporating automated systems that execute
intelligent O&M decision models.
In the O&M field, selecting an appropriate LLM, evaluating the effectiveness of model optimization,
and providing guidance for further optimization all require O&M capability assessment of LLMs.
The evaluation of LLM O&M capabilities should be based on different scenario tasks, selecting
corresponding evaluation datasets to assess the model’s performance, applicability, accuracy,
and effectiveness in practical O&M scenarios.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 258
Building an evaluation dataset
During the application of LLMs in the O&M field, standardized evaluation benchmarks are needed
to measure the performance and applicability of different LLMs. However, the O&M field lacks
authoritative benchmark datasets, making it difficult to effectively evaluate and compare the
capabilities of LLMs in this domain, as well as to clarify model optimization directions. In addition,
the diversity and quality of data are key factors affecting the effectiveness evaluation of models.
The following discussion uses Owl-Bench as one example of how an O&M-specific evaluation
benchmark can be designed and applied. To address the lack of standardized O&M benchmarks,
one domain-specific effort is Owl-Bench, developed by Yunzhi and Beihang University.
The paper Owl: A LLM For It Operations published at the International Conference on Learning
Representations (ICLR), 2024, constructed the high-quality O&M dataset Owl-Instruct and
the evaluation dataset Owl-Bench. Owl-Bench is a bilingual benchmark dataset consisting of
two different parts: a Q&A section with 317 entries and a multiple-choice section with 1,000
questions. It covers numerous real-world industrial scenarios in this field, ensuring the diversity
of Owl-Bench. The evaluation dataset includes nine different subdomains: information security,
application business, system architecture, software architecture, middleware, networks, operating

one part is free practice exams available online, and the other is carefully designed by experts
in the O&M field. All this data is not generated by GPT-like models and is preprocessed into the
form of Q&A and multiple-choice questions. The final statistical analysis results of Owl-Bench

Once an evaluation dataset has been defined, the next step is to choose scoring methods that
match the task type, such as accuracy for multiple-choice questions and human or model-assisted
scoring for open-ended answers.
Evaluation tools and methods
For evaluating LLMs in the field of O&M, it is necessary to obtain the performance ranking of
LLMs, analyze the number of model parameters and their impact on O&M performance, as well
as assess the improvements in O&M capabilities brought by prompt engineering, all based on
O&M Q&A evaluation criteria.
For the O&M evaluation benchmark, the customized benchmark dataset Owl-Bench was
chosen. The questions and prompts in the benchmark dataset are used to produce outputs
through the model, and the outputs are compared to the correct answers in order to assess the
model’s performance in the O&M domain. For multiple-choice questions, accuracy is used as
the evaluation metric; for subjective questions, recall, precision, GPT-4 scoring, expert scoring,
and other standards are adopted. It should be noted that the evaluation metrics for subjective
questions are highly dependent on manual effort and have poor scalability. Scoring via GPT-4
can be used to assess the match between the model’s answer and the reference answer.
A total of 994 multiple-choice questions were selected for evaluation, covering 9 O&M capabilities
(middleware O&M, information security O&M, infrastructure O&M, application and business
O&M, operating system O&M, database O&M, system architecture O&M, network O&M, software
architecture O&M). Each model’s responses to the multiple-choice questions were used to
separately calculate the accuracy for each of the 9 O&M capabilities. The accuracy for a single
O&M category is the number of correctly answered questions in that category divided by the total
number of questions in that category; the overall model O&M capability is the average accuracy
across the 9 O&M categories. During model loading, it is necessary to define different classes, use
different loading methods and model parameters to ensure the model is adapted to O&M Q&A
and able to demonstrate its best performance.

During the evaluation process, prompt engineering was compared to assess its improvements to
O&M capabilities, using a few-shot method and recording the number of reference Q&A examples
included in the prompt with ntrain. When ntrain=5, five Q&A pairs are included in the prompt;
when ntrain=0, no examples are included. Error outputs were statistically analyzed and mainly
divided into three categories: incorrect answers, unanswered, and output requirements not
met. Particularly when ntrain=0, the model outputs lack references, so corresponding prompts
must be debugged to ensure the model can answer every question. The test results show that

After defining the benchmark, scoring criteria, and prompt settings, the evaluation results can
be used to compare model performance across different O&M domains.
Evaluation results
In this benchmark, the strongest results were obtained by Qwen1.5-32B-Chat and Yi-34B-Chat.
Because Owl-Bench is bilingual and the evaluation set is tailored to O&M scenarios, these results
should be interpreted in the context of the benchmark design and model set evaluated.
Under several existing open-source LLMs, for the 994 multiple-choice O&M questions, the
single-category accuracy and average accuracy of each model were calculated, with the results
as follows: Qwen1 � 5-32B-Chat performed the best overall, with an average accuracy of 90.47%.
It also performed best in information security O&M, application and business O&M, operating
system O&M, system architecture O&M, and network O&M. qwen_72B_int4 performed best
in the middleware O&M domain, with an accuracy of 85.93%, but its average accuracy was only
83.96%. Yi-34B-Chat performed best in infrastructure O&M and database O&M, with an average
accuracy of 87.67%. In summary, the models with stronger O&M capabilities are Yi-34B-Chat
and Qwen1 � 5-32B-Chat. Related statistical analysis results are shown in Figure 7.24.
These results should be read as benchmark-specific findings rather than universal
rankings. For readers, the lesson is the evaluation method: define representative
O&M tasks, choose appropriate metrics, compare models across subdomains, and
interpret results in the context of the dataset and model set.

After evaluating how LLMs perform across general O&M tasks, the chapter now turns to a more
complex operational scenario: root cause analysis in microservice systems. Microservices create
highly distributed environments where faults can spread across services, dependencies, logs,
metrics, and traces. This makes root cause analysis a strong use case for multi-agent methods,
where different agents can analyze separate signals, share findings, and work together to identify
the likely source of a failure.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 262
Applying multi-agent root cause analysis to
microservices
In today’s development of internet technology, microservices architecture has become a
mainstream system design pattern. Microservices architecture breaks down a large system into
multiple independent, small services that can run and be deployed separately. These small services
communicate with each other over a network. Each microservice is usually built around a specific
business function and can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently of other services.
This architecture enables enterprises to rapidly adapt to market changes, achieving continuous
innovation and improvement. However, these advantages of the microservices architecture also
come with a series of challenges, especially in terms of system monitoring and fault diagnosis.
In a microservices environment, the system consists of dozens or even hundreds of independent
services, which may be distributed across different servers or containers, interacting with each
other through lightweight network communications. A common example of a microservices
architecture is shown in Figure 7.25.
Figure 7.25: Example of a typical microservices architecture

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops

chunks.content:
Chapter 7 263
This high level of decentralization and dynamism makes monitoring the system status, diagnosing
problems, and tracing faults much more complex. Traditional fault detection and root cause
analysis methods often struggle to cope with the complexity of microservices architectures, so
new technical solutions are required to improve the efficiency and accuracy of fault handling.
Because root cause analysis in microservices requires teams to examine alerts, service dependencies,
metrics, logs, and possible propagation paths at the same time, it is difficult for a single model
or rule-based workflow to handle the process effectively. Multi-agent systems address this by
dividing the investigation across specialized agents that can coordinate their findings.
Multi-agent systems
In recent years, artificial intelligence technologies, especially machine learning and LLMs,
have shown tremendous potential in various fields. Root cause analysis tools based on these
technologies can help technical teams quickly and accurately identify and resolve issues. In
particular, the concept of Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) offers a new perspective for addressing
complex problems within microservice architectures. In a multi-agent system, each agent is an
independent entity with its own goals and capabilities, able to collaborate with other agents to
accomplish complex tasks.
By combining the capabilities of LLMs with the collaboration of multi-agent systems, the industry
is experimenting with designing an efficient fault detection and root cause analysis framework.
In this framework, each agent acts as an independent LLM, responsible for processing different
specific tasks such as receiving and analyzing alerts, exploring dependencies between services,
assessing fault probabilities, etc. In this way, agents collaboratively form an automated process
from receiving alerts to identifying the root cause of failures, not only improving the efficiency
of fault handling but also enhancing the accuracy of fault diagnosis.
Implementations of multi-agent systems for IT operations typically use frameworks
such as Microsoft AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph, or OpenAI’s Swarm pattern, each
providing different trade-offs between developer control and orchestration auto -
mation.

occurring at node A, with the root cause node being I and the failure propagation path being I
G D A. This approach turns root cause analysis into a coordinated workflow: one agent
may receive and classify alerts, another may explore service dependencies, another may estimate

Application cases of multi-agent systems
One practical implementation of a multi-agent root-cause-analysis workflow includes the
following roles: when a service fails, related alerts are sent to the monitoring system, and the
issue is ultimately resolved through root cause analysis. The workflow is shown in Figure 7.27.
Figure 7.27: Workflow of multi-agent system
The workflow begins with alert intake and prioritization. The alert receiver acts as the first line
of defense in the system, responsible for receiving and handling alert events triggered by access
function blockages or monitoring system alarms. During this process, the alert receiver needs
to handle multiple alert events from different parts of the microservices architecture, covering
various types of failures. The alert receiver must perform a preliminary analysis of these alert
events, identify related alerts and false positives, as well as classify and prioritize the alerts. This
process requires the alert receiver to possess a high degree of intelligence and judgment to quickly
and accurately process large amounts of information.
After determining the priority of the alert events, the alert receiver forwards the most urgent and
impactful alerts to the process planner for further handling. The process planner is the core of
the entire system, responsible for coordinating the work of each agent, dividing the root cause
analysis tasks into multiple sub-tasks, and assigning these sub-tasks to other agents. This requires
the process planner to have strong coordination and decision-making abilities in order to allocate
tasks properly based on the actual situation and the capabilities of each agent.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 266
Once the process planner has divided the investigation into subtasks, the system moves into
evidence collection and dependency analysis. Under the coordination of the process planner, each
agent begins to execute their respective tasks. The data investigator is responsible for collecting
data from specified nodes, including average latency, traffic, error rate, resource saturation,
and concurrent user count, among others. This data provides important information for root
cause analysis. The data investigator must have strong data processing and analysis capabilities,
be able to extract valuable information from a large amount of data, and further analyze alerts
by collecting necessary contextual information, such as service logs, performance metrics, and
configuration change history.
The dependency explorer is responsible for analyzing the dependencies between nodes in the
microservices architecture. When the process planner receives an alert event requiring further
analysis, it sends a dependency request containing specific node information and alert time to

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 265
chunks.content:
the dependency explorer. The dependency explorer accurately identifies both direct and indirect
dependency nodes of the specified node through query tools and the global topology structure,
facilitating identification of fault paths, marking affected nodes, and developing further root
cause analysis and solutions. The dependency explorer needs strong analytical capabilities and
a deep understanding of microservices architecture, enabling accurate analysis of dependencies
between nodes. This step is critical, as in a microservices architecture, the failure of one service
often affects other services on which it depends.
After the relevant nodes and dependencies have been identified, the next step is to estimate which
nodes are most likely to be the root cause. The Probability Oracle is responsible for evaluating the
failure probability of each node within the microservices architecture. When the Process Planner
sends a request, the Probability Oracle analyzes the specified list of nodes to determine the failure
probability of each one. This process includes checking the accessibility of nodes: for inaccessible
nodes, the Probability Oracle will, by default, assign a higher failure probability. For accessible
nodes, the Probability Oracle evaluates the failure probability by calculation models based on
various performance metrics (such as response time, error rate, resource utilization, etc.). The
Probability Oracle must possess strong computational abilities and an in-depth understanding
of failure probability assessment models in order to accurately evaluate each node’s failure
probability. This process may involve multiple factors, such as the service’s historical failure data,
recent change records, and interaction patterns with other services.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 267
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 267
These probability estimates then need to be presented in a form that helps engineers understand
the fault network and propagation path. The Failure Visualizer is responsible for visualizing and
updating data in the pipeline. The Failure Visualizer receives failure probability information
from the Probability Oracle and updates the fault network accordingly. When the fault network
needs updating, the Process Planner sends a fault network request containing the nodes and their
corresponding failure probabilities. The Failure Visualizer creates or updates the fault network
based on this information, visually presenting the failure probabilities between different nodes.
The Failure Visualizer must possess powerful data visualization capabilities to clearly display
the status of the fault network.
Finally, the system moves from diagnosis to response by generating or recommending recovery
actions. The Solution Engineer is responsible for the final root cause analysis and solution
development. Once the root cause is identified, the Solution Engineer proposes repair suggestions
or automatically executes recovery operations, such as restarting services, rolling back recent
code deployments, or adjusting configuration settings to restore normal service operation as
quickly as possible. Specifically, after receiving the root cause analysis and solution request from
the Process Planner, the Solution Engineer formulates an action plan based on available node data.
If node data is available, the Solution Engineer conducts a metric-level analysis based on historical
data and performance metrics. If node data is unavailable, the Solution Engineer performs node-
level analysis by inspecting the topology of the microservices architecture to determine fault
impact. The Solution Engineer will also refer to successful cases to guide the development of the
current solution, and provide feedback information for further action and final resolution. The
Solution Engineer must possess strong problem-solving abilities and extensive experience to
develop effective solutions based on actual circumstances.
In addition to these individual agent roles, the overall system depends on coordination mechanisms
that allow agents to exchange information, review outputs, and reach a reliable conclusion.
At the same time, an efficient communication mechanism must be established between agents
throughout the multi-agent system in order to exchange information and coordinate actions.
Additionally, the system can integrate blockchain technology to enhance the transparency and
security of the decision-making process.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 268
In some implementations, governance mechanisms such as weighted voting or auditable decision
records can be added to improve transparency and accountability. Specifically, in this mechanism,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 267
chunks.content:
each agent can vote on the answer to any problem. For example, each agent can vote on the answer
to a problem, with voting weights determined by the agent’s contribution and expertise indices.
The contribution index reflects the agent’s activity and effectiveness in proposing suggestions
and voting, while the expertise index is based on the agent’s professional contributions and
action quality in specific fields. Through this voting mechanism, the system ensures that each
answer is approved by the majority of agents, enhancing the fairness and accuracy of the system.
With the widespread adoption of microservice architectures and the increasing complexity
of systems, traditional monitoring and fault diagnosis methods can no longer meet the needs
of modern software systems. The implementation of the entire process not only improves the
efficiency of fault handling, but also reduces the time and cost of problem resolution through
precise root cause analysis. In addition, the multi-agent-based root cause analysis framework
has good scalability and flexibility, allowing for the addition of agents or the adjustment of their
functions according to the actual needs of the system, so as to adapt to ever-changing technological
and business requirements.
By combining the advantages of LLMs with multi-agent systems, a more efficient and accurate
fault detection and root cause analysis framework can be built, helping enterprises better
manage and maintain microservice architectures and improve system stability and reliability.
This not only assists technical teams in quickly responding to and solving problems, but also saves
a great deal of time and resources for enterprises, thereby enhancing their competitive advantage.
Summary
In this chapter, you learned how LLMs can be applied to O&M scenarios such as log analysis,
intelligent troubleshooting, O&M knowledge base construction, ticket handling, capability
evaluation, and multi-agent root cause analysis in microservices environments. The chapter
showed how LLMs can help O&M teams detect anomalies, interpret complex logs, automate
responses, and improve operational efficiency through knowledge retrieval and agent-based
workflows.
Building on these ideas, the next chapter moves into testing scenarios, where you will learn how
LLMs can improve dynamic and static testing through automated test generation, program repair,
semantic code analysis, and vulnerability remediation.
8
Applying LLMs in Software
Testing
With the development of software engineering and the continuous improvement of product
quality requirements, intelligent testing technology plays a crucial role. As a cutting-edge branch,
intelligent, dynamic, and static testing are key means to improve test coverage and efficiency.
Moreover, while LLMs help drive the development of testing technologies, their application in

chunks.content:
testing scenarios still faces numerous pain points and challenges that need further resolution.
In this chapter, we will be covering the following main topics:
• Identifying pain points in software testing
• Improving dynamic and static testing with LLMs
• Addressing challenges in deploying LLMs for testing
• Building automated vulnerability repair with static analysis and RAG
Identifying pain points in software testing
Software testing is a critical stage in the software development process, and its effectiveness directly
determines the final quality of the software. Through comprehensive testing, developers can
eliminate potential errors and instability in the software, ensuring that the code implementation
meets the intended functional design. For different types of software and diverse testing goals,
R&D teams can choose from a variety of testing techniques, including unit testing, performance
testing, integration testing, smoke testing, compatibility testing, security testing, UI testing, and
stress testing.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 270
When we discuss how to apply LLM technologies in software testing scenarios, we must recognize
the significant differences between various testing techniques, and these differences can greatly
affect the effectiveness of integrating LLMs into testing.
From the perspective of testing principles, software testing techniques can be divided into two
categories: dynamic testing and static testing.
• Dynamic testing targets software in a running state, verifying its functionality, performance,
and security by actually executing the code. Common dynamic testing methods include
unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and performance testing. These testing
methods simulate user operations and scenarios, checking how the software behaves
and performs under different conditions, thereby uncovering runtime defects and issues.
To increase software feature coverage, dynamic testing typically requires writing a large
number of test cases to ensure as many system behaviors are triggered as possible.
• In contrast, static testing is conducted without executing the code, uncovering potential
issues through static inspection of code, documentation, and design. Common static testing
methods include code review, static code analysis, design review, and documentation
review. These approaches use manual checks or tools to analyze the structure, logic,
and compliance of the code to identify potential errors, code standard violations, and
optimization points, thus preventing defects at an early stage. Since software does not
run during static testing, it is impossible to obtain accurate runtime data, leading to
uncertainty in software analysis by static testing techniques. Especially for code with
more complex architecture and functionality, both the false positive and false negative

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 267
chunks.content:
rates are relatively high. In actual usage, R&D teams often need a substantial amount of
manual intervention to achieve better static testing results.
Whether it is dynamic testing or static testing, the purpose is to discover and fix defects and issues
in the software as much as possible before the software goes live. In modern software engineering
systems, these two techniques are usually used in combination to cover more testing scenarios
and comprehensively improve the quality and reliability of the software.
In summary, the application scenarios and technical logic of dynamic testing and static testing
are different, so the technical pain points and bottlenecks they face in practical applications also
differ. For example, for unit testing, the automatic generation of high-quality unit test cases will
directly impact its cost and effectiveness. For static testing, reducing the false positive rate is
the key to determining the usage cost of such tools. In addition, how to quickly extract effective
improvement and remediation solutions from the test results is also a common concern for
developers in both types of testing.

Having established that dynamic and static testing face different practical bottlenecks, the next
step is to examine how LLMs can support each approach. Dynamic testing benefits most from
improved test case generation and program repair, while static testing benefits from stronger
code semantic analysis, false-positive reduction, and vulnerability remediation.
Improving dynamic and static testing with LLMs
LLMs can support software testing in different ways depending on whether the testing process
involves executing the software or analyzing it without execution. Dynamic testing relies on test
cases, runtime behavior, execution feedback, and defect reproduction, while static testing depends
on code structure, rules, semantics, and analysis reports. Because these two testing approaches
have different workflows and pain points, this section examines them separately, beginning with
dynamic testing and then moving to static testing.
Intelligent evolution of dynamic testing
Before looking at how LLMs can improve dynamic testing, it is useful to first review how dynamic
testing works and where its practical limitations arise.
Tools by capability
LLM-augmented testing does not depend on a single tool or platform. In practice,
teams usually combine LLM-based assistance with the testing tools already used in
their development workflow. The following examples show common tool categories
that readers can use as a starting point:
• Unit testing frameworks: JUnit for Java, pytest for Python, Jest for JavaScript,
and Go test for Go
• Static analysis tools: Coverity, SonarQube, Semgrep, CodeQL, Infer, and
Klocwork
• Fuzz testing tools: AFL++, libFuzzer, Honggfuzz, and OSS-Fuzz
• LLM-augmented development and testing tools: GitHub Copilot for test
generation, Cursor, Sweep AI, and the experimental tools discussed in this
chapter, such as TestGen-LLM, Goshawk, and Corax
This list is not exhaustive. It is intended to help readers connect the chapter’s testing
concepts to familiar tool categories, such as unit testing, static analysis, fuzz testing,
vulnerability detection, and LLM-assisted code repair.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 272
Basic concepts of dynamic testing techniques
Dynamic testing technology is an important method in the field of software testing, aiming
to detect the functionality and performance of software through actual execution. Dynamic
testing requires the software under test to be in a running state, and guides software execution
of various operations and functions by means of manually or automatically constructed test
cases. By observing the software’s operating status, collecting test data, and deriving test results,
dynamic testing can effectively evaluate software quality. Generally speaking, dynamic testing
consists of the following key steps:

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 271
chunks.content:
1. Test Environment Preparation: The prerequisite for conducting dynamic testing is to
prepare one or more operating environments for the software under test and run the
software in these environments to ensure it can operate correctly. It should be noted
that whether the software can start normally in the operational environment is often
regarded as a key result of dynamic testing.
2. Test Case Construction: Before dynamic testing begins, testers need to design a series
of test cases that should cover the main functionalities of the software as well as various
low-probability scenarios that might occur. The generation of test cases needs to consider
specific software functions, different input data, the software runtime environment, and
other factors. When generating test cases, testers should make careful considerations as
much as possible to ensure that the dynamic testing process covers as many software
functions and code as possible. Code coverage is an important indicator of dynamic testing
and generally includes multiple dimensions such as statement coverage, branch coverage,
condition coverage, and path coverage. Depending on the software’s programming
language and type, testers typically select common tools such as JaCoCo, Cobertura,
and Istanbul to collect and analyze code coverage information during dynamic testing.
3. Test Case Execution: After completing the design and construction of test cases, testers
need to execute these test cases against the running software. Since test cases target
different software functionalities, both manual and automated execution of test cases are
common approaches. During the execution of test cases, collecting and recording software
runtime data is an important task. Testers should collect software runtime data as much
as possible, including runtime duration, memory consumption, CPU consumption,
input/output content, response speed, etc. The above data will be used to analyze and
produce the final test results.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 273
chunks.content:

4. Result Analysis: During the execution of test cases, testers need to record the execution
result of each case in detail. By analyzing these results, testers can uncover abnormal
behaviors during the software’s execution, thereby locating potential defects and issues
in the software. For example, some functionalities fail to operate as expected or produce
outputs that do not conform to the design under certain conditions.
5. Defect Reporting and Fixing: Based on the data collected during the testing process,
testers can promptly discover potential defects and issues in the software. Testers should
thoroughly document these issues and related information, and report them to the
development team. The development team should then fix these issues.
6. Regression Testing: After the issues have been fixed, testers should perform regression
testing to ensure that the fixes have not introduced new issues and that the original
functionalities continue to operate normally
Common dynamic testing techniques
Dynamic testing is a collective term for a class of testing techniques that require running the
software and interacting with and observing the software’s operating state to obtain results.
Common dynamic testing techniques are shown in Figure 8.1.
Figure 8.1: Common dynamic testing techniques
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 274
(1) Unit testing
The main goal of unit testing is to ensure that each module or function performs correctly and
can execute specific tasks as intended. This testing method provides fine-grained code checking
to ensure the reliability of fundamental components, thereby guaranteeing the overall correctness
and stability of the program.
(2) Integration testing
The main goal of integration testing is to verify whether the interaction between multiple
modules or components is correct. By combining different unit modules, it checks whether they
can work together after integration, ensuring the reliability and consistency of data transmission
and functional invocation between parts. Integration testing can identify and correct interface
issues and collaborative defects between modules early, thereby improving the overall stability
and functional completeness of the system.
(3) System testing
The main goal of system testing is to comprehensively verify the system’s functionality and
performance to ensure it operates as expected. This stage covers all aspects of the system,
including functionality, usability, performance, and security. Through system testing, it is
possible to discover software issues in the integrated environment and ensure that the system
can stably and efficiently provide the expected services during actual user usage.
(4) Regression testing
The main goal of regression testing is to ensure that the introduction of new code or the

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 273
chunks.content:
modification of existing code does not break the system’s existing functionality. This type of testing
repeatedly executes existing test cases, especially those related to the modifications, to validate
the system’s stability and reliability after changes. Effective implementation of regression testing
helps ensure that the system continues to maintain the expected functionality and performance
during continuous iteration and upgrades, preventing the introduction of new defects or issues.
(5) Stress testing
The main objective of stress testing is to assess the stability and reliability of the system under
extreme conditions. By applying extreme loads beyond the boundaries of normal operation, stress
testing aims to expose the system’s limits and weak points. Such tests help determine whether
the system can continue to operate under abnormal situations (such as sudden surges in traffic,
high concurrency, resource exhaustion, etc.) or if it can effectively recover from failures. Through
stress testing, potential risks and bottlenecks can be identified in advance, thereby enhancing
the system’s robustness and resilience.

(6) Performance testing
The main objective of performance testing is to evaluate the system’s speed, response time, and
resource usage. By designing and implementing a series of test scenarios, performance testing
helps identify and analyze the system’s behavior under various loads. This type of test focuses
on key performance indicators such as throughput, response time, CPU, and memory usage,
aiming to optimize system efficiency and ensure strong performance in real-world environments
to meet user needs. Performance testing effectively reveals performance bottlenecks in the system
and provides a basis for corresponding optimization and improvement.
(7) Security testing
The main objective of security testing is to discover and eliminate security vulnerabilities in the
system to ensure the safety of data and resources. By simulating various possible attack methods
and analyzing the system’s protection mechanisms, security testing evaluates the system’s ability
and robustness in resisting malicious attacks. This type of test covers potential security threats
such as authentication, authorization control, data protection, and network security. Through
security testing, potential security issues can be identified, security measures can be strengthened,
and the system’s integrity and confidentiality of data and resources can be effectively safeguarded
in the face of security challenges.
(8) Compatibility testing
The main objective of compatibility testing is to verify the software’s compatibility across a
variety of different environments (including operating systems, browsers, devices, etc.). By
testing the software on diverse software and hardware configurations and network environments,
it ensures consistency and stability across different platforms and devices. Such testing covers
compatibility across operating system versions, browser types and versions, mobile and desktop
devices, and even performance under different network conditions. Through compatibility testing,
environment-specific compatibility issues can be discovered, ensuring that the software meets
the needs of a broad user base regardless of their technical conditions.
(9) User interface testing
The main objective of User Interface Testing (UI Testing) is to verify the functionality and
appearance of the software’s user interface, ensuring a high-quality and consistent user
experience. By thoroughly testing the interactivity, layout, response speed, and visual consistency
of various interface elements, it can be confirmed whether they function correctly and comply
with design specifications. Such testing includes the functional behavior of buttons, text boxes,
menus, icons, dialogs, etc., as well as how the interface appears on different resolutions, window
sizes, and devices.

(10) Fuzz testing
Fuzz testing is a recently emerging testing technique whose primary goal is to uncover crashes,
abnormal behaviors, and potential security vulnerabilities in software. By automatically
generating large amounts of random or semi-random data and feeding it into the software, the
responses are observed to test how the software behaves under unexpected input. Such testing
effectively captures unforeseen edge cases and input combinations, thereby revealing issues that
may have been missed in conventional testing. Fuzz testing not only helps improve the stability
and reliability of software but also enables the early detection of security vulnerabilities that
could be maliciously exploited, enhancing the overall security and robustness of the system.
Pain points of dynamic testing
Although there are many types of dynamic testing technologies, we can still summarize some
common features from their technology stack, such as dependency on the environment,
requirements for real-time interaction, code coverage capability, and resource consumption.
Based on these common issues, current dynamic testing technologies face the following pain
points and bottlenecks in real-world scenarios:
• Limited Coverage: Traditional dynamic testing technologies struggle to achieve
comprehensive coverage of all possible code paths and user scenarios. The limitations in
coverage may result in certain potential bugs remaining undiscovered, leading to hidden
risks persisting even after the software passes testing, which affects end-user experience
and system stability.
• Difficulty Handling Complex Scenarios: When dealing with complex scenarios, dynamic
testing exposes significant limitations, especially when handling multi-threaded,
concurrent, and asynchronous operations. These complex situations are prone to cause
issues that are difficult to reproduce and diagnose, making it challenging for traditional
methods to address these tricky problems effectively.
• Resource Consumption: Real-time monitoring and analysis of software usually require
high system resources, particularly in terms of CPU and memory consumption. This has
a particularly significant impact on performance-sensitive applications. High resource
consumption not only increases the cost of testing but may also interfere with the normal
operation of the system under test.

• Limitations of Environment Simulation: The actual operating environments of different
software can be extremely complex, while traditional dynamic testing methods often
struggle to fully simulate all details of such environments. These limitations in simulation
capabilities result in test outcomes that may not be comprehensive or reliable enough,
thereby diminishing the effectiveness of the tests to a certain extent.
• Complexity of Data Analysis: The massive amount of data generated during dynamic
testing needs to be processed and analyzed to extract and utilize valuable information.
Traditional dynamic testing methods often cannot efficiently mine data and locate
problems due to technical and tooling limitations when handling and analyzing such
complex data.
• Heavy Dependence on Manual Effort: In traditional dynamic testing technologies, in
order to cover as many functions and scenarios as possible, the generation of test cases
often requires the participation of developers. Manually designed test cases not only
consume a great deal of time but are also prone to errors and inconsistencies. Worse yet,
this approach is rarely able to comprehensively cover all code paths and user scenarios,
potentially leaving certain functionalities or exceptional conditions insufficiently verified
and introducing risks. Such heavy reliance on manpower also makes it difficult for the
testing process to quickly respond to changing requirements or achieve automation,
further reducing the efficiency and quality of testing.
These pain points show why dynamic testing is a strong candidate for LLM-assisted improvement.
Since dynamic testing depends heavily on test case design, runtime feedback, defect analysis,
and repair, LLMs can be used to reduce manual effort and strengthen coverage in targeted parts
of the workflow.

Automated program repair

improve the accuracy and efficiency of problem resolution. By reducing manual intervention,

team, enabling developers to devote more time and energy to tasks that are more creative and
valuable, rather than being bogged down by tedious bug fixing. This not only boosts the team’s

Intelligent evolution of static testing
After examining dynamic testing, the discussion now turns to static testing, where software is
analyzed without being executed. Static testing plays a different role in the quality-assurance
process: instead of observing runtime behavior, it examines code structure, rules, dependencies,
semantics, and potential vulnerabilities before the software runs. This makes it especially useful for
early defect detection, but it also introduces challenges such as false positives, rule maintenance,
and difficulty interpreting complex code.
Basic concepts of static testing techniques
In addition to dynamic testing techniques, static analysis is another fundamental method in
software testing. Static testing detects potential issues and defects by analyzing the software
code without actually running the program. Since static analysis can be carried out in the early
stages of software development, it has unique advantages in identifying errors, vulnerabilities,
and bad practices in the code. The key steps of static analysis are shown in Figure 8.5.
Figure 8.5: Key steps of static analysis
1. Code Review Preparation: Testers need to prepare the codebase to be analyzed, ensuring
its completeness and correctness, and configure the relevant static analysis tools. The code
review preparation stage may also involve preprocessing steps such as code formatting
and comment cleanup, in order to improve the accuracy and readability of the analysis.
In this chapter, “static testing” refers specifically to automated static analysis tech -
niques; manual reviews and walkthroughs are out of scope.

2. Selection of Static Analysis Tools: The effectiveness of static analysis tools is closely
related to the programming language used by developers, the project scale, and specific
requirements. Common static analysis tools include SonarQube, Pylint, ESLint, FindBugs,
etc. These tools can automatically scan code, identify potential issues, and generate
detailed reports. Choosing the right tool is key to successful static analysis, as different
tools vary in their detection capabilities and performance.
3. Defining Rules and Standards: Before performing static analysis, a set of code quality
rules and standards needs to be defined. These rules usually cover coding conventions,
naming conventions, security checks, performance optimization recommendations, and
so on. By clearly defining the rules, the consistency and reliability of the analysis results
can be ensured. Many static analysis tools provide predefined rule sets and also allow
users to customize rules to meet specific needs.
4. Executing Static Analysis: After preparation is complete, testers use the selected tools
to perform static analysis on the codebase. The tools scan the code, apply the predefined
rules, identify potential issues, and generate reports. The execution of static analysis is
usually automated, but in some cases, manual intervention may be required to handle
complex code structures or specific business logic.
5. Result Analysis and Reporting: The reports generated by static analysis tools contain
issues found in the code, including errors, warnings, and suggestions. Testers must
analyze these results in detail to determine which issues actually need to be addressed.
The result analysis phase also involves determining priorities so that the development
team can focus on the most important issues. Static analysis reports not only help identify
code defects but also provide concrete suggestions for improving code quality.
6. Issue Fixing and Verification: Based on the static analysis results, the development team
needs to fix the code. After the fixes are completed, the static analysis tool is usually run
again to verify whether the issues have been resolved. This process may require multiple
iterations until all critical issues are resolved. Through repeated static analysis and fixing,
the code quality and reliability can be significantly improved.
7. Continuous Integration and Static Analysis: To ensure consistent code quality
throughout the development lifecycle, static analysis should be integrated into the
Continuous Integration (CI) process. Static analysis is automatically triggered on each
code submission or merge and, based on the results, determines whether the code is
allowed to enter the main branch. By combining static analysis with the CI/CD process,

continuous monitoring and improvement of code quality can be achieved.

Once the basic workflow is clear, it becomes easier to see how static testing techniques differ by
what they examine in the code. Some techniques focus on syntax and style, while others analyze
semantics, security risks, complexity, or dependencies.
Common static testing techniques
According to the technology used and the analysis objectives, common static analysis techniques
can be categorized into the following six types:
Syntax Analysis
The main goal of syntax analysis is to check whether the code conforms to the syntax rules
of the programming language. By parsing the code, syntax analysis can detect syntax errors,
unclosed parentheses, undefined variables, and other issues. Syntax analysis is the foundational
step of static analysis, ensuring that the code can be properly compiled or interpreted. With
the development of basic tools such as compilers, pure syntax analysis is no longer common
in software development processes. More often, syntax checking is used in conjunction with
analyzers to detect more complex issues such as security vulnerabilities.
Semantic analysis
Semantic analysis builds upon syntax analysis by further checking the semantic correctness of
the code. It focuses on issues such as variable types, scopes, and parameter matching in function
calls. Semantic analysis can detect type errors, uninitialized variables, invalid function calls,
and similar problems. Through semantic analysis, it can be ensured that the code is logically
reasonable and executes as intended. However, traditional static testing techniques cannot cover
data such as comments and variable names that contain complex semantic information, resulting
in incomplete semantic analysis of the code.
Code style checking
The main goal of code style checking is to ensure that code adheres to predefined coding standards
and style guides. By checking code formatting, naming conventions, and comment styles, code
style checking can improve the readability and consistency of code. Common code style checking
tools include ESLint (JavaScript), Pylint (Python), Checkstyle (Java), and others.
Security analysis
The main goal of security analysis is to discover security vulnerabilities and potential risks within
the code. By analyzing the security of the code, it is possible to detect common security issues such
as SQL injection, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), buffer overflows, and others. Security analysis tools
usually combine static analysis and pattern-matching techniques, providing detailed security
vulnerability reports. Common security analysis tools include SonarQube, Fortify, and others.

Complexity analysis
The main goal of complexity analysis is to assess the complexity of code, including loop
complexity, conditional complexity, and coupling between modules. By analyzing code
complexity, high-complexity areas that may be difficult to maintain and test can be identified,
guiding the development team to refactor and optimize code. Complexity analysis is relatively
common in embedded industries where software runtime resources are limited.
Dependency analysis
The primary goal of dependency analysis is to examine the dependencies between code modules
to ensure that module coupling remains within a controllable range. By analyzing dependencies,
issues such as circular dependencies and unused dependencies can be identified, thereby
optimizing code structure and improving the maintainability and scalability of the system. At
the same time, dependency analysis can also identify security issues introduced by dependencies
by comparing with third-party vulnerability databases and similar data sources.
Although these techniques can detect many issues early and operate efficiently across large
codebases, static testing still faces important limitations in real production environments.
Pain points of static testing techniques
Compared to dynamic testing techniques, static testing techniques demonstrate significant
advantages in code coverage, operating costs, and concurrency efficiency. However, when applying
static analysis tools in actual production environments, there are still many pain points and
challenges. These challenges not only affect the practical effectiveness of the tools but also impose
higher demands on the workflows of development teams.
• High False Positive Rate: Static analysis tools often generate a large number of false
positives, meaning the reported problems do not actually exist. A high false positive rate
not only increases the extra workload for developers but may also diminish their trust
in the analysis results, thereby affecting the tool’s practical effectiveness. Frequent false
positives force teams to spend more time filtering true errors from false positives, gradually
eroding developers’ enthusiasm for and trust in static analysis.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 288
• Maintenance of the Rule Set: The core of static analysis relies on a set of predefined
rules. These rule sets must be continuously updated and maintained to adapt to rapidly
changing programming language features and emerging security threats. Maintaining the
rule set is not only a massive workload but also requires a deep reservoir of professional
knowledge. This poses a serious challenge for development teams, both in terms of
time management and technical resource allocation. Given the fast-paced evolution of
programming languages and frameworks, promptly updating rule sets is crucial; otherwise,

analysis tools may fail or generate frequent false positives.
• Difficulty Handling Complex Code: When faced with complex code structures, static
analysis tools may demonstrate certain limitations, especially when analyzing advanced
programming features such as polymorphism, dynamic typing, and reflection. These
complex features may make it difficult for static analysis tools to accurately understand
the program’s behavioral logic, resulting in inaccurate analysis results. As a result, not
only is error localization and resolution more challenging, but it may also complicate
issues further, thereby reducing the practical value of the tool.
• Performance Overhead: When handling large codebases, static analysis tools often
require significant computational resources and time to perform in-depth scans. High
performance overhead not only lengthens analysis time and reduces development
efficiency but can also have a notable negative impact on continuous integration processes.
Especially in continuous integration environments, lengthy analysis processes can delay
the entire development workflow, seriously affecting product release schedules and team
productivity.
• Environmental Dependencies: Static analysis tools typically have specific requirements for
the development environment and system configuration. This increases the complexity
of integrating and using the tools. In diverse development environments, environmental
dependency issues may lead to inconsistent analysis results. For example, the same static
analysis tool may yield different analysis results in different development environments,
making problem localization and resolution more difficult.
• Complexity of Data Analysis: Reports generated by static analysis tools often contain
large amounts of data, and parsing this data requires technical expertise. Development
teams must be able to extract useful information from complex reports and turn it into
actionable improvements. Avoiding information overload and improving the readability
of reports are key to making static analysis results more useful.

• Tool Compatibility: Due to functional differences among static analysis tools, choosing
and integrating multiple tools to obtain comprehensive results can be difficult. Poor
compatibility can lead to fragmented or inconsistent findings, making it harder for
developers to interpret and act on the results. Improving tool compatibility and the overall
utility of static analysis workflows is therefore an important part of making static testing
more effective.
These pain points explain why LLMs are being explored as a way to make static testing more useful.
Rather than replacing static analysis tools, LLMs can help interpret code semantics, summarize
analysis results, reduce false positives, and support vulnerability repair.
Applying LLMs to static testing
Similar to dynamic testing, LLMs (LLMs) also demonstrate great potential in the field of static
testing and can provide assistance across a variety of static testing scenarios. For example, bugs
and vulnerabilities discovered during static testing typically require a significant amount of
manpower and time to fix, whereas LLMs can greatly simplify this process. By automatically
identifying and repairing vulnerabilities, similar to automated repair solutions in dynamic testing,
the application of LLMs can significantly reduce the time and resources development teams
spend handling these issues.
In addition, LLMs also show great potential in code semantic analysis and false positive
elimination. Through deep learning and natural language processing technologies, the models
can understand the complex semantic structures of code, accurately identify variable types,
function calls, and logical relationships, thereby greatly improving the accuracy of semantic
analysis. Moreover, LLMs can learn and identify common false positive patterns, using contextual
understanding and pattern matching to filter out irrelevant alerts and dramatically reduce false
positive rates. This not only increases the accuracy and reliability of static analysis tools but also
reduces the burden on developers, ultimately improving overall development efficiency and
code quality.
Code semantics analysis
Traditional static program analysis techniques mainly rely on the analysis of structured information
such as code and configuration files, often neglecting the complexity of code in terms of semantics
and logic. However, bugs and security vulnerabilities in modern software are not only related to
code structure and syntax but are also directly associated with software logic and code semantics.
These hidden problems are often difficult to detect in the early stages of testing, but once triggered,
they can pose significant threats to the stability and security of the system.

The emergence of LLMs provides R&D teams with new tools for deeply understanding code

semantics. LLMs possess excellent natural language understanding capabilities and the ability
to parse unstructured data, enabling them to analyze complex logic and semantics within code.
By combining LLM technology with traditional static analysis techniques, we can accurately
understand software logic during static testing and enhance the ability to identify deeper issues.
This combination not only increases the efficiency of vulnerability detection but also improves
its comprehensiveness and accuracy.
In 2022, a research team from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Feiyu Technology published a
paper titled Goshawk: Hunting Memory Corruptions via Structure-Aware and Object-Centric Memory
Operation Synopsis. This paper discusses how to utilize artificial intelligence technologies to identify
functions related to memory operation semantics, thereby enhancing the capability of static
analysis tools in detecting logical vulnerabilities in memory operations.
The development of modern C/C++ software increasingly relies on custom memory management
functions, especially in embedded R&D fields such as automotive and semiconductors. These
custom functions are responsible for allocating and releasing memory, but their custom behavior
may differ from the standard malloc and free functions, for example, by involving complex
operations such as multi-object allocation or nested allocation. This poses a challenge to traditional
static analysis techniques, as they usually focus only on standard memory management functions
and assume that allocation and release operations always occur in pairs.
To address this issue, this paper designs and implements a memory vulnerability detection tool
named Goshawk by combining traditional program analysis techniques with artificial intelligence
technologies. Goshawk aims to solve the analytical difficulties brought by custom memory
management functions.

As shown in Figure 8.6, Goshawk’s workflow includes the following steps:
Figure 8.6: Goshawk’s workflow
1. Identification of memory management functions: First, Goshawk uses natural language
techniques to scan and analyze the source code, extracting semantic features from function
prototypes and labeling the functions by category. Then, for each candidate function
classified as a memory management function, in-depth data flow analysis is performed
to verify whether they indeed execute memory allocation or release operations.
2. MOS generation: For each identified memory management function, Goshawk tracks
its managed memory objects using data flow analysis techniques and generates the
corresponding MOS representation as defined by MOS. MOS includes the function
name, attributes (such as allocation or release), a list of managed memory objects, and
the structural relationships between the objects.
3. MOS-enhanced vulnerability detection: Goshawk utilizes MOS information to optimize
data flow analysis and detect memory corruption vulnerabilities in an object-centric,
structure-aware manner. When analyzing a memory management function, Goshawk
directly uses the MOS information to update the state of memory objects, thereby avoiding
redundant analysis of code within the function.

By creatively integrating traditional program analysis with artificial intelligence technologies,
Goshawk performed excellently in the final experiments. In tests on 7 open-source projects,
Goshawk successfully analyzed over 273,000 lines of code and discovered 92 brand-new memory
corruption vulnerabilities, including use-after-free and double-free vulnerabilities. Compared
with traditional vulnerability detection tools, Goshawk’s analysis speed increased by several
orders of magnitude, and the generated vulnerability reports were clearer and more concise,
helping developers more easily understand and confirm vulnerabilities.
This paper combines natural language processing techniques with traditional static analysis
techniques to achieve automatic identification and precise detection of custom memory
management functions and memory corruption vulnerabilities, effectively addressing the
shortcomings of traditional program analysis technologies in dealing with complex logical
vulnerabilities. This research provides an innovative solution and new perspectives for the field
of software static testing. By integrating natural language processing with static analysis methods,
it significantly improves the efficiency and accuracy of the analysis process, demonstrating the
broad application prospects of LLM technology in software testing and security fields.
Beyond improving semantic understanding, LLM-based methods can also address one of the

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 291
chunks.content:
most persistent problems in static testing: distinguishing real issues from false positives.
Intelligent false positive elimination
In the field of static testing, a high false positive rate has always been a major pain point for
developers. Traditional static analysis tools rely on predefined rules and pattern matching, making
them prone to false positives when dealing with complex or dynamic code structures. In addition,
the lack of runtime information prevents static analysis from accurately determining the actual
behavior of code during execution, further increasing the likelihood of false positives. Advanced
code features such as polymorphism, reflection mechanisms, and dynamic types also pose
challenges for static analysis tools to fully understand the real intent and context of the code. The
maintenance and updating of rule sets is difficult, making it even harder for these tools to adapt
to new technologies and new language features. However, as LLM technologies emerge, there is
hope for breakthroughs in this situation. LLMs, leveraging deep learning and natural language
processing technologies, can better understand the results of analysis tools and identify false
positives, significantly reducing the false positive rate and improving the accuracy and reliability
of static analysis tools.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 293
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 293
In 2023, a research team from South Korea published an academic paper entitled False Alarm
Reduction Method for Weakness Static Analysis Using BERT Model, which proposed a defect analysis
false positive reduction method based on the BERT model and decision tree, as shown in Figure 8.7.
Figure 8.7: False positive reduction method for defect analysis based on the BERT model and
decision tree model
The system constructed by the authors of the paper first preprocesses the source code, including
cleaning out useless comments, blank lines, and so on, and standardizes defect annotations. Then,
the BPE algorithm is used to break the source code into smaller units, such as words, punctuation
marks, etc., and each word is converted into a vector representation, with positional information
added to help the model understand the structure and semantics of the code. The preprocessed
data is used to train the BERT model and decision tree model, where the BERT model is used to
analyze the code line by line, identify potential defects, and utilize the attention mechanism to
calculate the relevance scores between defect code lines and other code lines; the decision tree
model is used to classify the output of static analysis tools and determine whether each warning
is a false positive. Finally, the trained models are applied to new code to identify potential defects
and use the decision tree model to reclassify the output of static analysis tools, thereby reducing
the false positive rate and improving the efficiency and accuracy of defect analysis.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 294
The paper’s authors selected six common static analysis tools— Cppcheck, Clang Static Analyzer,
Flawfinder, Infer, Frama-C, and PVS-Studio —to test the effectiveness of this framework. These
testing tools are based on different static analysis techniques, such as lexical analysis, type
inference, data flow analysis, symbolic execution, theorem proving, and model checking. By
integrating the output results of these tools, defects in the source code can be analyzed more
comprehensively, thereby improving the accuracy of defect analysis. At the same time, the paper
uses the NIST Juliet test suite C/C++ version 1.3 as the test dataset. This suite contains a large
amount of known defect code and normal code, which enables effective evaluation of the model’s
performance. During the experimental process, the authors first used the selected static analysis
tools to perform defect analysis on the test dataset and mapped and grouped each tool’s output
results to CWE. Then, the BWA model was used to analyze each line of code in the test dataset,
and the ACM model was used to classify the analysis results. Finally, metrics such as the false
positive rate were calculated to evaluate the model’s performance.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 293
chunks.content:
The experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively reduce defect analysis
false positives and improve the efficiency and accuracy of defect analysis. The BERT model
performs excellently in the line-by-line defect analysis task, with high accuracy, precision, and
F1 score. It can effectively identify lines of code with potential defects and utilize the attention
mechanism to analyze the relationship between defective lines and other lines, thereby more
accurately judging the severity of defects. The decision tree model also performs well in the alert
classification task, with high accuracy, precision, F1 score, and AUC. It can effectively identify false
positives and reclassify the output results of static analysis tools, thus reducing the false positive
rate. Compared to using a single static analysis tool, this method can more comprehensively
analyze defects in source code and improve the accuracy of defect analysis. For example, for
Buffer Over-read (CWE-125) defects, the false positive rate with a single tool is 79%, while with
this method, the rate drops to 7%. For Use of Uninitialized Variable (CWE-457) defects, the
false positive rate drops from 93% to 11%. The false positive reduction effect of this method varies
across different defect categories, but overall, it can significantly reduce the false positive rate,
improve the efficiency and accuracy of defect analysis, and provide important technical support
for secure software development.
LLMs can improve both dynamic and static testing, but their value depends on how reliably they
can be deployed in real testing workflows. Before adopting them at scale, teams need to consider
practical constraints such as context window limits, hallucinations, model selection, fine-tuning
costs, explainability, evaluation, and long-term maintenance.
