chunks.heading: Chapter 8 295
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 295
Addressing challenges in deploying LLMs for testing
This section provides an in-depth discussion of the application potential of LLMs in dynamic
software testing and static software testing. It demonstrates their powerful logical reasoning
capabilities, natural language processing skills, code generation abilities, and how they can
enhance the effectiveness and accuracy of traditional software testing techniques. Without a
doubt, LLMs show broad application prospects in the field of software testing. However, when we
attempt to apply LLMs in real-world software production environments, we still face numerous
complex technical difficulties and challenges. This section, drawing on practical experience in
deploying LLMs, will delve into these technical challenges.
Model reliability challenges
Before LLMs can be used reliably in testing workflows, teams must understand the core limitations
that affect model output, especially context window constraints and hallucinations.
Managing LLM context window limits
Currently, LLMs generally have limitations on the context input window when processing text
data. For example, GPT-4’s context input window is capped at 32,000 tokens. Although some
foundational LLMs claim to handle ultra-long contexts, their ability to “find a needle in a haystack”
and “maintain focused attention” in the face of massive amounts of data still requires further
validation. As a result, in software testing scenarios, LLMs may encounter insufficient input
window issues when analyzing longer code fragments or test data, making it difficult for the
model to directly address complex testing requirements and results.
A feasible solution is to use other analytical techniques to segment and structure the data before
feeding it to the LLM, and then input the data into the model step-by-step via RAG or Agent
technologies. This approach can effectively alleviate the limitations of the processing window
and enhance adaptability to complex tasks. For example, splitting code by functional modules
and then incrementally inputting them into the LLM for analysis can help improve processing
efficiency and accuracy.
Reducing hallucinations in testing workflows
Since the emergence of LLMs, they have often been plagued by the issue of “ hallucination.”
When LLMs handle problems with frequent context switching, complex logical reasoning, and
a large amount of mathematical computation, they frequently provide irrelevant answers or fail
to understand the logic of the question. This phenomenon results in an inability to fully trust the
output of LLMs when using them to assist in software testing. Currently, it remains technically
difficult to completely resolve this issue at the foundational level.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 296
Current coping methods include secondary verification and filtering of the LLM’s outputs, or using

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 295
chunks.content:
Agent technology to break down a single question and answer into multiple reasoning chains
(such as CoT) and recall verification processes. If resources permit, multiple LLMs can be used to
handle the same task, and the results can be cross-validated to improve accuracy. For example, in
the code review process, using several LLMs to independently analyze the same section of code
and comparing the analysis results can help to better identify potential problems.
Deployment and architecture choices
Once the main reliability risks are clear, the next step is choosing the right deployment pattern,
model, and adaptation strategy for the testing task.
Choosing between RAG and agent-based workflows
RAG and Agent technologies are the two most common forms in which LLMs are applied to
specific tasks. Agent here refers to the LLM-driven orchestration pattern introduced in Chapter 7,
where the model autonomously plans steps, calls tools, and iterates on results.
RAG, by combining retrieval and generation, is particularly suitable for tasks that require high-
quality text generation, such as question answering systems and dialog generation. It retrieves
relevant information from a predefined knowledge base, combines it with the input information,
and generates the final output. This enhances contextual understanding and reduces the
probability of generating inaccurate or unreasonable content.
In contrast, Agent technology executes specific tasks through autonomous intelligent agents.
These agents can perceive their environment (such as application state, user input, etc.), make
decisions, and perform corresponding actions based on predefined rules or learned strategies,
and continuously adjust their strategies and behaviors through feedback mechanisms to adapt to
different testing environments and requirements, thereby achieving automation of complex tasks.
In the field of software testing, due to the wide variety of tasks and diverse principles and
requirements, it is particularly important to flexibly choose between RAG or Agent technology.
For example, when dealing with tasks that have few steps but require extremely high accuracy
of results, RAG technology is more appropriate; while for systematic tasks that require multiple
steps and frequent context switching, Agent technology achieves better results. For instance,
in automated regression testing, Agent technology can flexibly cope with changing testing
environments, improving test coverage and efficiency.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 297
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 297
Selecting the right foundation model
LLM technology is developing rapidly, and foundation models with different numbers of
parameters and various pre-training tasks are emerging one after another. Models ranging from
1 billion to 200 billion parameters exhibit varying inference performance and efficiency depending
on the task. In software testing tasks, choosing the most suitable model to achieve the best results
at the lowest computing cost is particularly important. For example, for integration testing of
complex systems, selecting a large-parameter model may yield better inference performance, while
for simple unit testing, a smaller-parameter model can be chosen to save computing resources.
In addition, some enterprises have strict data security management mechanisms and do not
allow core data (such as code) to be sent to the cloud for processing. In such cases, it is necessary
to consider the feasibility of deploying LLMs locally, balancing computing power and cost while
ensuring data security. For example, a localized and streamlined LLM can be deployed and
combined with the enterprise’s own data security strategies, thereby better protecting data
privacy and security.
After selecting a suitable base model, teams must decide whether the model’s existing capabilities
are sufficient or whether fine-tuning is needed for testing-specific tasks.
Deciding whether to fine-tune LLMs
Fine-tuning LLMs is an effective way to significantly improve their performance on specific
reasoning tasks. Experiments show that fine-tuned LLMs demonstrate obvious enhancements
in tasks such as code explanation and program repair. However, as the base models develop,
their parameter counts, and the scale of training corpora increase rapidly—models with up to
100 billion parameters considerably raise the cost of fine-tuning. In addition, these base models
already cover most common corpora during pre-training, including code, and software testing-
related data, so the performance improvement from fine-tuning may gradually diminish.
Therefore, whether to fine-tune a base model and whether it is cost-effective requires a
comprehensive trade-off based on the situation. For example, when handling common code review
tasks, one may choose not to fine-tune but instead directly leverage the pre-trained capabilities
of LLMs; however, when working on testing tasks in specific domains, proper fine-tuning can
significantly boost performance.
Improving model performance is only one part of deployment. In testing workflows, teams also
need to understand why a model produced a recommendation and whether testers, developers,
and security teams can trust the result.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 298
Operational governance
After an LLM-based testing workflow is deployed, teams need processes for explaining results,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 297
chunks.content:
measuring performance, and maintaining the system over time.
Improving explainability and transparency
The explainability and transparency of LLM reasoning processes have not yet been fully addressed.
In software testing scenarios, the application of LLM technology usually involves collaboration
across multiple departments, and different users (such as testers) need to understand and trust
the results output by the model. This places higher demands on the explainability, predictability,
and transparency of the LLM’s reasoning process. In practical applications, how to enable relevant
personnel to understand and trust the model’s outputs is a highly challenging issue.
Ways to address this problem include introducing explainability techniques such as SHAP (Shapley
Additive Explanation) or LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation) to analyze
and demonstrate the decision basis of LLMs. At the same time, increasing transparency reports
and thoroughly documenting the training process, data sources, and application scenarios of
LLMs can help users gain a clear understanding of the model’s performance and limitations.
Beyond explaining individual outputs, teams also need a systematic way to measure whether
LLM-assisted testing improves accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and cost-effectiveness across
real workflows.
Evaluating LLM performance in test scenarios
When implementing new technologies in real production environments, most companies and
teams wish to conduct a detailed assessment of the costs and benefits of the technical solutions
before actual application. As a new technology in the field of software testing, LLMs have a
technical core and usage methods that are completely different from traditional technologies.
How to perform accurate and effective performance evaluation for LLMs has become an urgent
and important issue to address.
On this basis, enterprises need to establish a comprehensive evaluation framework covering
multiple dimensions such as accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. For different testing tasks,
appropriate evaluation metrics and methods should be formulated. For example, in functional
testing, the performance of LLMs can be evaluated by comparing the detection rate and false
positive rate of automated testing tools; whereas in performance testing, efficiency can be
measured by analyzing the response time of LLMs under different loads.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 299
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 299
Maintaining and updating LLM-based testing systems
The implementation and toolification of LLM technology means it will become an important part
of the daily toolchain for software testing teams. In daily use, how to continuously maintain the
availability of LLMs, and as usage deepens, how to continuously iterate LLM solutions to improve
their effectiveness, are issues that urgently need to be explored.
In addition, with the advancement of computing power and technology, the foundational
models previously used need to be upgraded and replaced. How to smoothly transition to new
foundational models, especially synchronizing the optimization experience accumulated by
old models to the new ones, remains a complex problem. Therefore, it is necessary to formulate
systematic maintenance and update strategies to ensure that the performance and stability
of models are not affected during the upgrade process, while also effectively addressing model
degradation and data drift issues. For example, regularly conducting model validation and
regression testing, monitoring changes in model performance, and promptly adjusting and
optimizing model parameters can ensure the efficient and reliable operation of LLMs in practical
applications.
After examining the broader challenges of deploying LLMs in testing workflows, the discussion
now turns to a concrete application: automated vulnerability repair. This example shows how
static analysis, retrieval-augmented generation, and LLM-based code generation can be combined
to locate vulnerabilities, provide the model with relevant context, and produce repair suggestions
that developers can review and apply.
Building automated vulnerability repair with static
analysis and RAG
In the software development process, security vulnerabilities remain a pervasive issue that
demands close attention. As software systems become increasingly complex, both the number,
and types of vulnerabilities grow, which presents significant challenges to developers and
enterprises. Traditional manual vulnerability repair methods are not only time-consuming
and labor-intensive, but they also place high demands on developers’ security knowledge and
experience, while requiring substantial time and effort investment. This approach is prone to
errors during execution, which may lead to the emergence of new vulnerabilities or even affect
the normal operation of existing functionalities.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 300
Manual vulnerability repair is costly, involving not only labor costs but also the time and resources
consumed during the repair process. For large software projects, the cost of repairing vulnerabilities
is especially significant, often becoming a major burden in development and maintenance.
To address the limitations and high costs of manual vulnerability repair, LLM technology offers

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 299
chunks.content:
an innovative and efficient solution. By leveraging LLM technology, we can achieve automated
vulnerability repair. LLMs have significant advantages in natural language processing and code
generation, allowing them to automatically identify and fix various types of security vulnerabilities.
Specifically, the application advantages of LLM technology in automated vulnerability repair are
mainly reflected in the following aspects:
• First, LLM technology can greatly improve the efficiency of vulnerability repair. Traditional
manual repair methods often require repeated code review and testing, while LLM
technology can quickly identify and repair vulnerabilities through its powerful analytical
capabilities. This can significantly reduce the workload for developers during the repair
process, making it more efficient.
• Secondly, using LLM technology can reduce the cost of vulnerability repair. Automated
repair reduces dependency on human resources and shortens the time required for repair.
In addition, LLMs can process large amounts of code and vulnerabilities in a short period,
substantially lowering time and resource costs and increasing overall production efficiency.
• Finally, LLM technology can reduce errors that may occur during the repair process. Due
to its advantages in data processing and pattern recognition, LLMs can avoid many
omissions and mistakes that may occur in manual repair processes, ensuring the accuracy
and reliability of vulnerability repair and improving the overall security of the software.
The following workflow uses Corax as one example of how a static analysis tool can support
automated vulnerability repair. The same general pattern can also be implemented with other
static analysis tools, where the tool identifies vulnerabilities, supplies structured context for RAG,
and helps convert model output into reviewable repair suggestions. Coverity, SonarQube, Semgrep,
CodeQL, Infer, and Klocwork are similar static analysis tools commonly available. Figure 8.8 shows
the system architecture and workflow of the Corax system for automated vulnerability repair.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 301
chunks.content:
Chapter 8 301
Figure 8.8: Workflow of an automated vulnerability repair pipeline
The specific workflow is divided into three main steps: vulnerability localization, generating
LLM prompt, and processing model output.
Vulnerability localization
First, leveraging Corax’s powerful vulnerability scanning capabilities, static analysis is performed
on the source code to automatically identify security vulnerabilities in the code. To improve the
accuracy and reliability of LLMs during the vulnerability repair process, Corax not only performs
conventional static code analysis but also conducts more detailed data modeling of the source
code. When generating vulnerability reports, Corax stores contextual information related to each
vulnerability in a database. This data includes the code snippets triggering the vulnerabilities,
involved functions and variables, and related configuration file information. The purpose of this
is to reference this detailed information during subsequent prompt engineering, significantly
reducing potential hallucinations by the LLM, thus improving the accuracy of vulnerability repair.
Once the vulnerability and its relevant code context have been localized, the next step is to package
that information into a prompt that the LLM can use to generate a repair.
Applying LLMs in Software Testing 302
Generating LLM prompt
After the user selects the vulnerabilities to be automatically repaired, Corax aggregates all data
required for repairing those vulnerabilities. This data covers detailed vulnerability information,
relevant code snippets, code context information, and associated knowledge from the security
vulnerability knowledge base. This data serves as the RAG query results, entering the next step
of prompt engineering. The LLM will systematically organize this data according to a preset
format, including the user’s specific requirements and questions, then send it to the underlying
LLM interface. The key in this step is to ensure that the input information provided to the LLM is
comprehensive and accurate, enabling it to generate high-quality repair suggestions.
After the LLM generates a repair suggestion, the system must convert the output into a form that
developers can inspect, verify, and apply safely.
Processing model output
After the LLM generates repair suggestions, Corax continues to process these outputs. First, Corax
converts the repair code generated by the LLM into natural language explanations, including an
analysis of the vulnerability’s cause and a detailed description of the repair strategy. This step
not only helps developers understand the root cause of the vulnerability and the repair method,
but also verifies the correctness of the repair code produced by the LLM. Next, Corax converts the
repair code returned by the LLM into more practical formats, such as code diff or git pull/request,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 301
chunks.content:
making it easier for developers to apply these repair suggestions. Specifically, the code diff format
clearly displays the modified parts of the code, facilitating comparison and verification during
code review; whereas the git pull/request format can be directly applied to the code version control
system, further simplifying the repair process.
The above three steps constitute the core process of Corax’s automated vulnerability repair.
By fully leveraging the natural language processing and code generation capabilities of LLMs,
as well as detailed data modeling and prompt engineering techniques, efficient, and accurate
automated vulnerability repair is achieved, providing strong support for developers. This system
not only improves the efficiency of vulnerability remediation and reduces remediation costs, but
also significantly enhances the accuracy and security of the repair process, providing important
technical means for modern software development and security assurance.

Summary
In this chapter, you learned how LLMs can be applied to testing scenarios to improve both dynamic
and static testing, from automated test generation and program repair to semantic code analysis,
false-positive reduction, and vulnerability remediation. You also explored the practical challenges
of deploying LLMs in testing workflows, including hallucinations, context window limits, model
selection, fine-tuning, and evaluation.
Building on this testing-focused use of LLMs, the next chapter shifts to programming scenarios,
where you will learn how large code models support code generation, code completion, project-
level development, and developer productivity across real software engineering workflows.
9
Applying Code LLMs in
Software Development
Large code models, often implemented as code-focused LLMs, are AI models trained on large-scale
code datasets and designed to handle code-related tasks. These models are typically based on
deep learning architectures represented by Transformers, and are trained through pre-training
objectives such as language modeling. Through training on massive amounts of code data, the
models can improve code writing efficiency and quality, and assist in code understanding and
decision-making.
In this chapter, we are going to cover the following main topics:
• Defining large code models and their core characteristics
• Exploring common code LLMs
• Mapping downstream code tasks
• Tracing the evolution of code generation and completion
• Identifying pain points in code generation and completion
• Applying agent-based methods to project-level code generation
Defining large code models and their core
characteristics
With the rapid development of information technology, software development is becoming
increasingly important in various fields. As an emerging technology in the field of artificial
intelligence, large code models bring unprecedented opportunities and changes to software
development. Understanding the definition and characteristics of large code models is crucial to
fully leveraging their advantages and promoting the intelligent process of software development.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 306
Large code models are based on deep learning technology, and through learning and training
on massive code datasets, they can understand, generate, and optimize code. They do not

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 8 303
chunks.content:
simply recognize code syntax and structure, but can also capture semantic information, logical
relationships, and programming patterns within code. For example, large code models, such
as Codex, Code Llama, etc., can generate corresponding code snippets based on given natural
language descriptions or modify and improve existing code.
Large code models possess characteristics such as large-scale data-driven learning, deep
understanding of code semantics, strong generative ability, self-adaptivity and optimization
capabilities, and cross-language support.
Large-scale data-driven
Large code models usually require a huge amount of code data for training, with data sources that
are broad and include open source projects, code repositories, software development platforms,
and so on. By learning from immense volumes of code, the models can master the syntax rules,
programming styles, and common code structures of various programming languages. For example,
the abundance of open source code on GitHub provides rich learning material for the models,
enabling them to learn the coding styles used in different domains and application scenarios.
Deep understanding of code semantics
Unlike traditional code analysis tools, large code models can deeply understand code semantics.
They are able to recognize relationships among elements such as variables, functions, and
classes in code, and understand the purpose and functionality of code. For instance, when the
model analyzes a segment of code that calculates the sum of two numbers, it can understand the
mathematical logic and the role of variables within it.
Powerful generation capabilities
Large code models are capable of generating new code based on given requirements or prompts.
This generative ability not only includes simple functions and modules, but also complex system
architectures and complete applications. For example, users only need to describe the functional
requirements of software, and the model can generate the corresponding code framework and
core code logic.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 307
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 307
Adaptive and optimization capabilities
Large code models can adaptively adjust the generated code according to different programming
tasks and contexts, thereby improving the quality and efficiency of the code. They can also
optimize the generated code, such as optimizing algorithms and improving code readability and
maintainability. For instance, when handling performance-critical code segments, the model can
automatically choose more efficient algorithms and data structures.
Cross-language support
Many large code models possess the ability to understand and generate across multiple
programming languages, enabling code conversion and migration between different languages.
For example, a model that can handle Python, Java, and C++ code simultaneously can help
developers reuse and integrate code between projects in different languages.
These characteristics explain why large code models are increasingly being adopted as practical
development assistants rather than remaining purely research tools.
As shown in Figure 9.1, the 2023 Developer Survey Report data indicates that 44% of developers
have already used AI tools in the development process, and 77% of respondents support making
AI tools a part of the development workflow.
Figure 9.1: Data on the use of AI tools
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 308
This growing adoption reflects three main ways large code models can support developers and
development teams:
• Improving Development Efficiency: In terms of improving development efficiency,
developers can quickly obtain code examples, solutions, and code snippets by interacting
with large code models, significantly reducing development time and workload
• Lowering the Development Threshold: Regarding lowering the development threshold,
for beginners and non-professional developers, large code models can provide assistance
and guidance, helping them enter the software development field more easily
• Driving Innovation: In terms of driving innovation, large code models can inspire new
programming ideas and innovative solutions, bringing new possibilities to software
development
After defining what large code models are and why they matter to software development, the next
step is to look at the major models that have shaped this field. Comparing these models helps
show how different organizations have approached code generation, completion, reasoning, and
developer assistance.
Exploring common code LLMs
This section introduces five representative code LLMs: Codex, AlphaCode, StarCoder 2, Code
Llama, and DeepSeek Coder. This section introduces five influential code-focused models and
coding assistants that illustrate different approaches to code generation, completion, reasoning,
and developer support. The following examples show different directions in code-focused model

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 307
chunks.content:
development: natural-language-to-code generation, competitive programming, open-source
code models, multilingual code completion, and repository-level understanding.
Codex
In August 2021, OpenAI released a machine learning software called Codex. This software can
translate English into code, aiming to reduce the workload of professional programmers and
help amateurs with coding.
Codex is an AI-based code generation tool that can automatically generate corresponding code
snippets based on developers’ requirements. Trained on massive code repositories, Codex is
capable of writing code in multiple programming languages, including Python, Java, C++, and
more. In the development process, Codex significantly improves coding efficiency, reduces errors,
and allows developers to focus more on implementing business logic.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 309
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 309
Codex has code completion capabilities and can predict the subsequent code based on code
snippets already entered, thus helping developers quickly finish their code. This feature is
especially useful for beginners, providing timely hints, and guidance while coding. In addition
to code completion, Codex can generate complete code snippets based on developers’ descriptions.
For example, you only need to tell Codex you want to implement a sorting algorithm, and it will
generate the corresponding code for you. This is very useful for rapid prototyping or solving specific
problems. Codex can also optimize existing code to improve its runtime efficiency. By analyzing the
code’s structure and performance bottlenecks, it provides corresponding optimization suggestions.
Many applications are based on Codex, such as code assistants Copilot, Pygma, and Replit. Copilot
can generate code based on instructions, convert comments into code, generate tests, and provide
alternative solutions. Pygma uses Codex to convert Figma designs into high-quality code. Replit
uses Codex to describe the functionality of selected code segments, making it easier to understand
their purposes.
AlphaCode
In 2022, the renowned programming competition site Codeforces published an article titled
AlphaCode (DeepMind) Solves Programming Problems on CodeForce, which brought AlphaCode
into the spotlight and once again put DeepMind at the top of major media headlines. This was
DeepMind’s next revolutionary product after successfully launching AlphaGo in 2015—which
defeated the world’s best Go players—to change the world again.

AlphaFold, Google’s AI company DeepMind has launched another groundbreaking programming

DeepMind states that AlphaCode has achieved a very competitive level in writing computer

in the top 54%, marking an important step forward for humans toward autonomous coding.
According to DeepMind’s official website, AlphaCode is an AI tool developed by Google’s UK AI
division. The tool is capable of participating in major programming competitions and has the
ability to solve new problems involving critical thinking, logic, algorithms, coding, and natural

in programming competitions. Codeforces holds one or two algorithm competitions each week
and features a unique ladder ranking system. After participating in 10 Codeforces programming

Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 310
StarCoder 2
StarCoder 2 is a code LLM based on the Transformer architecture, designed to handle natural
language and generate source code in multiple programming languages. This series of models
includes three versions, with parameter sizes of 3 billion, 1 billion, and 15 billion, all trained on
the Stack v2 dataset. The Stack v2 dataset is seven times the size of Stack v1 and contains a vast
amount of code, questions, answers, discussions, and mathematical formulas from platforms such
as GitHub, Stack Overflow, Codeforces, and others. It covers 619 programming languages, ranging
from low-resource languages (such as COBOL) to high-resource languages (such as Python).
The StarCoder 2 code LLM family is trained on multiple programming languages and can perform
specialized tasks such as source code generation, workflow generation, and text summarization,
helping developers improve work efficiency. For example, when developers input natural language
requirements, the model can generate corresponding code snippets. In addition, the model can
perform self-learning and optimization based on user feedback, thereby improving the quality
and readability of the generated code.
Compared with the previous generation StarCoder model, the StarCoder 2 model has been
optimized for performance; its 3 billion parameter version already approaches the performance
of the original 15 billion parameter StarCoder model. This is due to a new training technique
employed by StarCoder 2 called CodeBERTa, which improves the model’s generalization and
understanding of programming languages without increasing parameter count. The CodeBERTa
technique combines contrastive learning and masked language models, utilizing a large amount
of unlabeled code data to achieve successful pre-training and fine-tuning of code. StarCoder 2
also features advantages in transparency and cost-effectiveness, as the series uses the BigCode
Open RAIL-M license, allowing users to access and use the models without paying royalties.
Code Llama
Meta’s open-source Llama model family welcomes a new member, Code Llama, a foundational
model focused on code generation. The release of Code Llama addresses the only programming
shortcoming of Llama 2, aiming to enhance code completion abilities and handle programming
tasks. The model is fine-tuned from the Llama 2 base model and comes in three versions: base,
Python, and instruction-following. Each version offers three parameter sizes: 7B, 13B, and 34B.
Notably, the 7B parameter model can be run on a single GPU. In multiple code benchmark
evaluations, Code Llama achieved state-of-the-art performance among open models, with scores
of 53% and 55% on HumanEval and MBPP, respectively. Code Llama’s performance is comparable

Chapter 9 311
DeepSeek Coder
DeepSeek Coder is an open-source code LLM designed to provide powerful code generation, code
completion, and mathematical reasoning capabilities. Its training dataset is mainly sourced from
GitHub, covering 87 programming languages, and undergoes a strict data processing pipeline,
including filtering and selection to ensure high data quality. The model uses various parallel
strategies during pre-training to optimize computational efficiency, including tensor parallelism,
ZeRO data parallelism, and pipeline parallelism. In addition, the model is instruction-tuned to
enhance its ability to handle long contexts.
In the multilingual programming tests on the internationally authoritative HumanEval dataset,
DeepSeek Coder outperformed existing open-source models across various languages. Compared
with Code Llama, DeepSeek Coder achieved a lead of 9.3%, 10.8%, and 5.9%, respectively, in code
generation tasks. Notably, DeepSeek Coder with 7 billion parameters matches the code capability
of Code Llama at 34 billion parameters. Moreover, after instruction tuning, the DeepSeek Coder
model even surpasses GPT3.5-Turbo, demonstrating strong mathematical and reasoning abilities.
The technical features of DeepSeek Coder include the first-ever construction of repository-level
code data and the use of topological sorting to parse dependencies between files, significantly
enhancing the ability to understand long-range and cross-file contexts. Additionally, by
incorporating the Fill-In-Middle method, it greatly improves code completion capabilities.
These techniques enable DeepSeek Coder to surpass the open-source benchmark Code Llama 3
in multiple tasks, such as code generation, cross-file code completion, and solving math problems
through programming.
aiXcoder
aiXcoder is a widely used AI coding assistant in the Chinese market. aiXcoder is an
intelligent programming assistant based on deep learning code generation tech -
nology, developed by Silicon Heart Technology, aimed at improving programmers’
coding efficiency. The product automatically predicts programmers’ intentions,
continuously recommending “the next segment of code to be written”, allowing
programmers to confirm the upcoming code input directly with “one-click com -
pletion”, thus greatly enhancing coding efficiency. aiXcoder can intelligently search
and recommend standard code for functions similar to the current program during
programming, providing strong reference for programmers.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 312
After introducing representative code LLMs, it is useful to look at the kinds of programming tasks
these models are designed to support. These downstream tasks show how code LLM capabilities
are applied in practice, from generating code from natural language to summarizing, translating,

repairing, and reasoning about existing code.
Mapping downstream code tasks
According to the definition of software engineering, downstream tasks of code can be classified
based on the input-output patterns of code into five types: text-to-code, code-to-code, code-to-
text, code-to-pattern, and text-to-text. The application of LLMs in programming has expanded
from simple single-step tasks, such as code generation and completion, to more complex scenarios
that combine retrieval, repair, testing, reasoning, and cross-file context understanding. In practice,
exploration of some deep domain features often involves combining different downstream tasks
of code, ultimately forming scenarios that better fit business needs, as shown in Figure 9.2.
Figure 9.2: Usage scenarios of code processing tools
The aiXcoder R&D team originates from the Key Laboratory of High Confidence
Software Technologies (Peking University), and it is the first Chinese intelligent
programming assistant based on deep learning code generation technology. As of
March 22, 2022, aiXcoder’s community edition has developer users in more than 130
countries and regions, providing intelligent programming services to over 300,000
international developers. In addition, aiXcoder has launched versions for Android,
JFinal, TensorFlow, and more, offering support to programmers in different fields.

chunks.content:
Chapter 9 313
The first category begins with tasks where natural language is used to retrieve, generate, or guide
the creation of code.
Text-to-code tasks
Text-to-code tasks take text as input and output code, typically involving scenarios such as code
retrieval, code generation, and numeric programming:
• Code Retrieval: Aims to search for relevant code based on natural language, or to mine
parallel text-code pairs from unannotated corpora. This task is usually accomplished
by computing the similarity between the query and candidate code embeddings, and
contextual embeddings produced by bidirectional language models (such as BERT) have
been proven to be very useful.
• Code Generation: Aims to generate code based on natural language descriptions, typically
functions or methods. This task can be seen as an upgraded version of code retrieval,
utilizing generative models instead of retrieval models. Statistical Machine Translation
(SMT) and Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have been widely applied to this
task, often with enhanced decoders utilizing the unique syntactic rules of programming
languages. However, pretrained language models based on the Transformer architecture
have changed this landscape, allowing direct source code generation via autoregressive
language modeling even without task-specific fine-tuning.
• Numeric Programming: Numeric programming is also a special case of code generation,
requiring the language model to solve mathematical reasoning problems by generating
code that will be executed by an external interpreter. This task abstracts the reasoning
process from numerical calculation, so this should be given special consideration when
choosing a code LLM or in practice.
After tasks that generate code from text, the next category focuses on transforming, completing,
repairing, or testing existing code.
Text-to-SQL is a special case of code generation, and this approach is sim -
pler. The model generates SQL commands from natural language queries;
compared to general-purpose languages such as Python and C, SQL has
structured characteristics. Therefore, the text-to-SQL approach has been
widely used in data management.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 314
Code-to-code tasks
Code-to-code tasks take code as input and output code, usually including scenarios such as code
search, code completion, code translation, code repair, and code infilling.
• Code Search: Code search is a task similar to code retrieval. The difference is that the
input consists of existing code fragments, and the programming language used is usually
different from the target language.
• Code Completion: Code completion aims to complete a segment of code based on a given
code prefix. This essentially applies language modeling to code, and related technologies

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 313
chunks.content:
such as N-gram, RNN, and Transformer have gradually been introduced. However, due to
the structured nature of programming languages, many early studies found that syntax-
assisted statistical models performed better, and neural models only became mainstream
after 2018.
• Code Translation: The goal of code translation is to translate a segment of code (usually a
function or method) into another programming language. The relationship between code
translation and cross-language code search is similar to that between code generation and
text-to-code retrieval, and SMT/MNT models are also widely applied to this task. Code
generation can help programmers write code snippets, but code translation is different;
it is an important technology for migrating old projects written in outdated languages.
However, we have not yet seen such applications, because even for such projects, the
context window of the most powerful language models is still quite limited.
• Code Repair: Code repair, also known as bug fixing, aims to fix erroneous code. Like code
translation, it is also a traditional code-to-code task, with Cloze tests as a typical example.
Cloze tests are code processing tasks proposed after the rise of BERT-style pre-training.
Owing to the specific semantics of programming languages, this test usually selects several
keywords such as min and max.
• Code Infilling: Code infilling is another task put forward after the popularity of
intermediate infilling pre-training. It is a scenario of code completion, where not only
the left context is given, but also the right context. However, it differs from the Cloze test
in that the Cloze test targets only a single token, while code infilling can target entire
lines or even multiple lines, which requires the decoder to generate them automatically.
• Unit Test Generation: The purpose of unit test generation is to generate unit tests for a
given program. Before the emergence of Codex and other code LLMs, almost all work in
this field used non-neural approaches. However, in the era of LLMs, this task is becoming
increasingly important. Research shows that the current unit tests used to evaluate the
program generation capabilities of code LLMs may not be sufficient.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 315
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 315
• Assertion Generation: Assertion generation is a task closely related to unit testing. Given a
program and a set of unit tests, the goal of this task is to generate assertions (also known
as oracles in software engineering) so that the program can be evaluated using the unit
tests. This task is not typically the focus of the NLP community, as program generation
tasks for LLM evaluation generally involve independent, competitive approaches, where
simply asserting that the program output matches the expected answer suffices.
• Mutation Generation: The purpose of mutation generation is to produce mutants of
a given program for mutation testing, which is closely related to unit test generation
and assertion generation. Mutants that are not detected by a given set of unit tests and
assertions indicate the need for additional test cases or better assertions. Masking tokens
in the source code and sampling from the output of masked language models has become
a common approach for this task.
• Fuzz Testing: Fuzz testing aims to mutate a given set of unit tests to generate new test cases
and is another task related to software testing. While much of the fuzzing work targets
deep learning libraries, very few have utilized language models to carry out this process.
• Type Prediction: Aims to predict types in dynamic programming languages such as Python
and JavaScript. It has been used as a pre-training objective for code LLMs and is often
simplified to a binary tagging task to predict which tokens in the code are identifiers.
Some downstream tasks move in the opposite direction, using code as the input and producing
natural language descriptions, reviews, or labels.
Code-to-text tasks
Code-to-text tasks take code as input and output text, typically including scenarios such as code
summarization, code review, and identifier prediction.
• Code Summarization: Code summarization, also known as docstring generation, aims
to generate a natural language description for a given piece of code (usually a function
or method). This is the exact opposite of code generation, and SMT/NMT techniques
are also applied here.
• Code Review: Code review aims to automate the process of peer code reviews, and it comes
in various forms. Many early studies formulated it as a binary classification task to accept
or reject modifications upon submission, while other studies used information retrieval
techniques to recommend comments from existing comment repositories. However, as
generative models have become more powerful, researchers have also explored directly
generating review comments as a sequence-to-sequence learning task.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 316
• Identifier Prediction: This is the task of predicting the names of identifiers in the code.
Since these names are believed to contain important semantic information, this task has

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 315
chunks.content:
been used for code summarization as well as for the pre-training of code models.
Beyond generating or describing code, code LLMs can also help identify patterns, similarities,
and reasoning structures within code.
Code-to-pattern tasks
Code-to-pattern tasks involve classifying code, typically including scenarios such as clone
detection and code reasoning.
• Clone Detection: This predicts whether two pieces of code are clones of each other. In
software engineering, there are four types of code clones, with the most difficult to identify
being semantic clones —code with different syntax but identical functionality. As this
task can be framed as a sentence pair classification problem, BERT-style language models
have been widely used in this area.
• Code Reasoning: This is a recently introduced downstream code task. This task requires
the model to perform reasoning on code or algorithms and answer related questions
presented in multiple-choice form. The questions may cover areas such as conceptual
understanding, numerical computation, and complexity analysis.
Finally, some programming-related tasks operate mainly on technical text rather than source
code itself.
Text-to-text tasks
Text-to-text tasks take text as input and output text, typically including scenarios such as
document translation and log parsing.
• Document Translation: This refers to the automatic translation of code-related
documentation. Since models, datasets, and prompt strategies for machine translation are
very rich in NLP, the technical implementation of document translation is not complicated.
• Log Parsing: This aims to analyze system logs generated by software products, such as
parsing logs into structured templates or detecting anomalies from raw logs.
After mapping the main downstream code tasks, it is useful to focus on one of the most important
and widely used areas: code generation and completion. Understanding how these technologies
developed helps explain why modern code LLMs are able to move beyond simple token suggestions
toward context-aware code assistance, functional code generation, and project-level development
support.

Chapter 9 317
Tracing the evolution of code generation and
completion
Code programming assistance technologies have a history of more than 40 years. Their
development has gone through several stages, from syntax highlighting, integration within
integrated development environments (IDEs), to code analysis and specification checks.
Among these, tools such as IDEs have been iconic over the past 20 years. They significantly
improve development efficiency and quality through features like automatic code completion,
code highlighting, syntax error prompts, and code snippets, while also delivering a superior
programming experience to developers.
LLM technologies have achieved remarkable breakthroughs and success in general industries,
especially excelling in natural language processing tasks. General-purpose LLMs typically possess
some programming capabilities. However, since their training data mainly consists of general
natural language texts—while programming languages are more structured, have explicit
syntax rules, and more direct and precise semantics—their performance in code understanding
and generation, which is a specialized field, may be limited to some extent. This characteristic
distinguishes them from general-purpose large models.
To better meet developers’ needs in code-related tasks, LLMs are trained on large-scale code
repositories, learning code snippets, programming patterns, and coding conventions, thus better
understanding code structure and logic and generating code that adheres to syntax and semantic
requirements.
In practice, how to effectively improve the efficiency and quality of software development has
always been a concern in the field of software engineering. Among various approaches, code
generation, and completion technologies are considered important methods for enhancing
software development automation and ensuring quality, attracting widespread attention from
both academia and industry. Code generation and completion refers to using certain techniques
to automatically generate source code for software, aiming to enable automatic programming
based on user requirements. This greatly reduces developers’ development burden and allows
them to focus more on delivering business value.
In academia, code generation and completion is an important branch of program synthesis,
aiming to assist, or even replace, programmers in writing code. Automatic generation of front-end
code is divided into two approaches: view code and logic code. Common solutions for generating
view code include automatic generation from design drafts, such as imgcook. Common schemes
for generating logic code include visual orchestration-based generation, input-output sample-
based generation, code corpus-based generation, and function description-based generation.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 317
chunks.content:
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 318
Common code generation and completion techniques
Code generation and completion techniques belong to program automation technology and are
also an important component of modern integrated development environments. Code completion
greatly improves programming efficiency and reduces spelling errors during the coding process.
Code generation and completion techniques typically help programmers predict class names,
method names, keywords, and so on. The prediction of the next token is the most common
form in code generation and completion processes, and is also the mainstream method used by
current IDEs. In common IDEs, the recommended tokens are often listed in alphabetical order,
which increases the time it takes for programmers to select a candidate token, often leading to
a suboptimal user experience.
Traditional code generation and completion approaches are mainly divided into two types. One
type utilizes static type information combined with various heuristic rules to decide which token
to predict, such as method names, parameters, etc. This method rarely considers the semantic
information from code context; for example, the mainstream code completion system in Eclipse
uses static category information to recommend Java methods to users, and the recommended
method names are usually sorted alphabetically. The other method leverages code samples
and previous semantic context to complete code. In 2009, Bruch et al., in the paper Learning
from Examples to Improve Code Completion Systems, described the use of the kNN (k-Nearest
Neighbor) algorithm to match the current completion semantics with previous code samples,
thereby improving completion accuracy. Techniques that use preceding semantic context for code
completion usually utilize special types of context information (such as the set of APIs being called)
to assist with completion. In 2010, Huo et al., in the paper Towards a better code completion system by
API grouping, filtering, and popularity-based ranking, proposed a code completion technique called
BCC. This technique implements Eclipse’s type-based code completion system by ranking and
filtering APIs. This approach usually requires manually defining many heuristic rules to specify
the set of contextual semantics, and if the semantic context at the current completion position
does not match the defined set, this method will fail.
Deep learning methods improve the accuracy of token recommendation by learning the probability
distribution among code tokens from large-scale codebases. The first proposal for probabilistic
modeling of code token sequences was presented by Hindle et al. in their 2012 paper On the
Naturalness of Software. Theoretically, programming languages are written by humans, exhibiting

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 317
chunks.content:
repetitive language patterns. Thus, they possess some predictable statistical features that can
be captured by language models. This hypothesis has become the cornerstone for applying
probabilistic models and even deep learning to learn programming languages.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 319
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 319
The most direct approach to next-token prediction is to use the program’s token sequence to
predict the current completion position, employing deep learning to accomplish code completion
as shown in Figure 9.3. This process mainly consists of two parts: the training phase and the code
generation and completion phase.
Figure 9.3: The workflow of code completion using deep learning
Researchers first collect a large amount of data from open-source code repositories or open-
source communities to serve as the corpus for deep learning. To learn from the code in the corpus
more effectively, researchers typically process the source code using code parsers, for example,
converting source code into token sequences or abstract syntax trees. Subsequently, researchers
select or design a deep neural network suitable for their specific task and train it using the data
from the corpus. Currently, the deep neural networks frequently used in code completion tasks
are language models; for example, recurrent neural networks can effectively learn the sequence
characteristics of programs and apply these features to code completion tasks. During the code
generation and completion phase, a partial code snippet is input, and the trained deep learning
model is invoked at the current completion point.
Code generation and completion technologies have developed through several technical paths,
each using a different kind of input, structure, or model to help produce code.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 320
Code generation and completion based on visual orchestration
Visual programming is not a new concept. From the earliest visual plugins to today’s low-code
and no-code technologies, all fall within the realm of visual programming. Visual programming
uses some componentized integrated code visualization platforms to allow so-called “junior
developers” who lack professional coding skills and development experience to independently
organize or participate in application development. In this way, code development expands
from a programmer-exclusive duty to a wider audience. It mainly allows programmers to use
various controls provided by the software itself to build various interfaces of applications in a
modular, building-block-like fashion. Visual orchestration is better suited for the generation of
interface view code.
Currently, there are many platforms that enable visual programming and low-code programming.
Typical representatives include OutSystems, Mendix, Salesforce, and Younuo Technology.
Similarly, there are also many visual solutions for relevant logic code: some are realized through
visual plugins, some through visual components, and others via low-code technologies.
Apart from business scenarios, some emerging fields also adopt visual coding as a business model,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 9 319
chunks.content:
such as simple logic programming for children. For enterprises, with market changes, business
logic, and system architecture are increasingly complex; personnel involved in related businesses
also need to possess a certain degree of reverse engineering thinking skills. Therefore, replacing
programming languages with graphical methods can improve the involvement of business
personnel in the software delivery process.
The advantage of current mainstream logical code visual orchestration solutions lies in highlighting
visual flow and the efficiency brought about by reusable logic nodes. The core is to break down
complex business processes, incorporating input/output and logic processing details into the
specific form rules of each business node. Figure 9.4 shows a complete logical orchestration process.

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 321
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 321
Figure 9.4: Visualized logic orchestration flow
Among them, node materials are used to define elements in the editor, including icons in the
toolbox, ports, and component schemas in the properties panel. The logic orchestration editor
is a visual editor that, based on the component information provided by the materials, edits and
produces JSON-formatted orchestration description data. The orchestration description data is
the output of user operations in the editor and is consumed by the parsing engine. The front-end
parsing engine, implemented in TypeScript, directly parses the “orchestration description data”
and executes it, thereby realizing the business logic of the software. The back-end parsing engine
can also directly parse and execute the “orchestration description data,” thus implementing the
business logic of the software.
Visual orchestration is suitable for scenarios with a high degree of logic reuse. The reusable
logic can be abstracted as nodes. The granularity of node reuse is crucial. If the granularity is as
large as a functional service, it can be considered business process orchestration. Scenarios with
high business process reuse are suitable for business parties to operate directly through visual
orchestration tools. If the granularity is as small as the expression level, it can be considered
business logic orchestration. A granularity that is too fine requires users to have a programming
mindset; in such cases, users with programming skills can achieve higher efficiency by writing
code directly.
While visual orchestration relies on reusable nodes and predefined flows, programming by
examples allows users to describe desired behavior through sample inputs and outputs.
Applying Code LLMs in Software Development 322
Code generation and completion based on input–output
examples
Automatically inferring and generating logic programs based on input-output examples is called
PBE (Programming by Examples). PBE is a subfield of program synthesis. The paper Program
Synthesis Using Natural Language proposed a technical solution for program generation. In practical
applications, there is an intuitive and easy-to-implement case of program generation, namely the
Auto-fill function in Excel. This function can quickly generate formulas for table items based on
several examples. For instance, in Figure 9.5, the values 2 and 4 in the first column can be used to
fill in even numbers, and the values 50 and 40 in the second column can automatically deduce
the result of an arithmetic sequence formula.
Figure 9.5: Illustration of generating table item formulas

In reality, the accuracy of the Auto-fill function for complex formulas or scenarios is less than
50%. The goal of PBE is to automatically infer computer programs to accomplish a task using
simple inputs and outputs. A 2017 paper proposed Neural Programming by Example (NPBE), a
deep-neural-network-based system that learns from input-output strings to induce programs
that solve string-processing problems. The architecture has four components: a string encoder, an
input-output analyzer, a program generator, and a symbol selector. NPBE solves some common
string processing problems in spreadsheet software systems through training.

Another path is to generate or complete code by learning from existing code corpora, where
repositories and snippets become reusable sources of programming knowledge.
Code generation and completion based on code corpora
The prerequisite for code generation and completion based on a code corpus is having a sufficient
corpus, which we often refer to as code snippets. Traditional IDE plugins have already initially
implemented the collection and analysis of common code snippets, which is a relatively common
way of analyzing a code corpus. With the development of code repository technology, analyzing
and utilizing the large amount of code accumulated in repositories to eventually form a company’s
core assets—transforming the value of code into proprietary technology and intellectual property—
has become a new direction for technological output. At the same time, combining code corpus
with management measures and deeply embedding code LLM technology into development and
management processes to form domain knowledge and management standards has become an
ongoing research topic for many enterprises, as shown in Figure 9.8.
